name: Yara Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at six in the control room of a large ore mine, then walk out to inspect the haul truck I operate. I have a vocational certificate, but most of what keeps a truck safe is listening to its engine and knowing when the haul road has turned slick. I use an AI app daily to sort my shift notes, although it cannot feel a tyre slipping. My partner Tomas works in a warehouse, and our two children keep asking whether I can come to their school events; the mortgage makes overtime hard to refuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the truck still needs a driver, even if software makes the log sheet quicker. The mine won't change its whole fleet just because a chatbot writes tidy notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would welcome a shorter paperwork queue, but the mortgage still has my attention every month. We have about three months of expenses saved, and a quiet production week can eat into that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep driving the day shift and use my AI app to draft handover notes, then check every number myself. In the first year I would put a fixed part of each overtime payment toward the mortgage rather than count on overtime forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about my place at the controls. I still don't love opening the mortgage statement after a month when the mine has slowed down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of a shift still needs your judgment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The app cannot tell me that the north ramp is loose under the tyres until I report it. I'd write that in the handover, as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home when overtime is light?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Tomas that we're keeping the children's swimming lessons, but we won't make a bigger holiday booking this year. I want room to breathe if a truck is down for repairs.

say: I'd say **The truck** still needs a driver, and quicker log sheets will not change the haul road beneath the tyres.
I would tell my crew that **small software gains** are useful when we check the numbers ourselves.
think: I would take **less paperwork**, but a quiet production week still puts pressure on our mortgage.
I think our **three months** of savings make a slowdown manageable for a while, though I would not spend that cushion lightly.
do: **Keep driving** the day shift and check every AI drafted handover number against the truck display.
**Pay down** our mortgage with a fixed portion of each overtime payment during the first year.
feel: **Steady** at the controls, with a little worry when overtime and mortgage payments meet.
S0.quote: The mine won't change its whole fleet just because a chatbot writes tidy notes.
fieldNote: Her **public confidence** rests on the physical judgment needed on a changing haul road.
Her **private worry** is ordinary production downtime against a mortgage, even in the least disruptive picture.

steps.text: Keep driving the day shift and checking truck handover numbers
Pay down the mortgage with part of each overtime payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the planners may lose more work than the drivers at first. If software can set routes and order parts, we'd better make sure it hears from people who actually drive them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office side would change before my cab does, and then management may expect one driver to cover more ground. I'm willing to learn a new dashboard, but I don't want a computer marking a rough road safe from a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the maintenance lead to show me the truck's condition screen and try the route tool with my own shift notes. In the first year after those tools arrive, I'd record every false safe-road alert and learn how to correct the route data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious, mostly, but I can see where a missed warning lands. A missed warning lands with whoever is in the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when a route recommendation looks wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the route tool sends me down the north ramp after rain, I'll stop and call dispatch. I would want that stop recorded, not treated as poor performance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger drivers to keep a paper record of bad route calls. The office may trust a clean screen more than a muddy windscreen.

say: I'd say **Planners** may see tasks move first, while drivers need a voice when route software sets the day.
I would welcome **better parts ordering** if the people driving trucks can correct bad road information.
think: I think management may use **new targets** to make each driver cover more ground before robots reach the cab.
I can learn a **condition screen**, but a safe label from an office cannot settle a muddy road.
do: **Ask maintenance** this month to show me the truck condition screen and test it against my shift notes.
**Record false alerts** during the first year and correct the route data with dispatch.
feel: **Curious**, with a sharp concern about false safe-road signals and pressure on drivers.
S1.quote: The office may trust a clean screen more than a muddy windscreen.
fieldNote: She treats **software** as something to test with firsthand road evidence, not as a badge of progress.
Her **safety concern** comes from tougher targets and bad route calls, while she does not expect immediate replacement by robots.

steps.text: Learn the truck condition screen with the maintenance lead
Record bad route calls while continuing day shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 could change dispatch and paperwork almost overnight, but a truck still needs us until capable robots arrive around 2031. I'd push for honest staffing plans instead of rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I would worry that the mine could freeze hiring and trim our overtime before any robot takes the wheel. The three-year gap sounds long until I count mortgage payments in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd build our savings from three months to five by banking overtime, and I'd ask to shadow the equipment technicians. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd seek paid training on truck sensors and fault checks while I still have driving shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried enough to move, not frozen. I can handle a new screen, but I cannot train a mortgage to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household expense would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas and I would cancel the autumn trip before we touched the children's swimming lessons. I would show him the numbers, not just tell him I'm worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make technical training worth your time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the maintenance lead whether sensor checks are part of the driver's job or a separate post. If it is a real post with wages attached, I'll apply to learn it.

say: I'd say **Thinking AI** could alter dispatch quickly in 2028, while capable truck robots are still about three years away.
I would ask the mine for **staffing plans** so the crew can act on facts instead of rumours.
think: I think a **hiring freeze** or lost overtime may hurt our mortgage before a robot reaches my truck.
I think the **three-year gap** is useful only if paid technical work exists when I finish learning it.
do: **Bank overtime** now until our household savings cover five months of expenses.
**Shadow technicians** and seek paid truck sensor training in the first year after thinking AI arrives.
feel: **Worried** enough to move, with a plan that depends on real technical openings.
S2.quote: I can handle a new screen, but I cannot train a mortgage to wait.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 thinking changes** from possible hands-on robot replacement around 2031.
Her plan depends on **paid training** and a real technician position; the family cannot finance a long unpaid course.

steps.text: Bank overtime until household savings cover five months of expenses
Shadow equipment technicians and seek paid truck sensor training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2031 gives us time to inspect what the software gets right before robots might drive around 2034. I would ask for a real training calendar, not a poster about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could move into maintaining the trucks if the mine offers proper supervised practice. But if every driver has the same idea, there may be fewer maintenance seats than people wanting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set aside two evenings a month to work through the equipment manuals with the maintenance lead, starting this winter. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I would apply for a paid technician apprenticeship and keep driving until I know its wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about a crowd all trying the same doorway. Five years gives me a better chance than two, if I actually use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wage would you need before changing roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't leave a typical driving wage for an unpaid title. I'd ask for the apprentice wage in writing before shifting the family budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the plan to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children know I drive the big trucks; I'd tell them I might become the person who keeps those trucks running. I would not promise that the job is there yet.

say: I'd say **Five years** lets drivers test new systems before capable truck robots might arrive around 2034.
I would press for a **training calendar** with supervised work and a wage stated in writing.
think: I think a **maintenance route** could suit me, but there may be fewer places than drivers seeking one.
I will keep the **driving wage** until an apprenticeship offer has real pay attached.
do: **Study equipment manuals** with the maintenance lead twice a month, starting this winter.
**Apply for** a paid technician apprenticeship in the first year after thinking AI arrives, while keeping driving shifts.
feel: **Uneasy**, though five years makes a practical trial possible.
S3.quote: I would ask for a real training calendar, not a poster about the future.
fieldNote: She sees the **2031 arrival** as a chance to test systems before hands-on robots arrive around 2034.
Her **job change** is conditional on a paid place and a known wage, not confidence that maintenance vacancies are guaranteed.

steps.text: Study equipment manuals with the maintenance lead twice monthly
Keep driving shifts until a paid apprenticeship wage is confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade is enough to make choices if we get clear information about the fleet. By 2036, dispatch and paperwork may be remade; the hands-on truck change is around 2039 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be in my mid fifties when the robots arrive, so I wouldn't plan on switching careers from scratch then. I'd rather have the mortgage nearly gone and a maintenance credential in my pocket before that point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a monthly payment above the mortgage minimum now and price a part-time equipment certificate this year. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd ask for sensor maintenance shifts, provided the course has led to recognized work at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel almost relieved by the time, though not by the destination. Ten years is enough for our children to finish school and for us to make a less desperate choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine sponsors the course, I'll enroll without draining our emergency fund. I won't drain our emergency savings to buy a certificate that the mine may not value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the old job would you keep if possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want to drive sometimes if the work exists. A tidy dashboard cannot feel a truck slide on wet gravel. Listening to a truck before a shift is a skill I don't want to lose just because a screen looks tidy.

say: I'd say **A decade** gives drivers room to plan before hands-on truck robots might arrive around 2039.
I would ask the mine for **fleet information** and course support before choosing a new role.
think: I think by my **mid fifties**, a fresh career change could be harder than moving gradually toward truck maintenance.
I want the **mortgage smaller** and a recognized credential before driving work may shrink.
do: **Pay extra** on the mortgage each month while checking the cost of a part-time equipment certificate.
**Enroll in training** if the mine sponsors it, then request sensor shifts after thinking AI arrives.
feel: **Relieved** by the planning time, while still sad at the thought of losing driving work.
S4.quote: I won't drain our emergency savings to buy a certificate that the mine may not value.
fieldNote: Her **long plan** pairs debt reduction with a possible recognized maintenance credential.
She will seek **mine sponsorship** if course fees threaten the emergency fund; the training route stays conditional.

steps.text: Pay above the mortgage minimum each month
Enroll in a part-time equipment certificate if the mine sponsors it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because overtime could disappear before I've built enough savings, and robots might reach the trucks around 2031. A paid path into equipment work, with the wage and places stated clearly, would help me plan without gambling the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a mine will listen when a driver says the road data is wrong. I'd want those calls recorded so a tidy dashboard never outranks a real hazard.

headlineQuote: A tidy dashboard cannot feel a truck slide on wet gravel.
portrait: **Yara Lopez**, 43, operates haul trucks at a large mine and supports two school-age children with her partner.
Her **vocational training** and daily AI use encourage testing, while the mortgage and three months of savings limit risk.
She expects **thinking AI** to change dispatch and records before capable robots reach hands-on truck work about three years later.
Across the pictures, she seeks **paid equipment training** and less mortgage debt, with each move tied to real wages and vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because lost overtime could arrive before she builds a larger cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid equipment path** with clear wages and available places would let her plan around the mortgage.
